prompt.context: Imagine you are consulting the CEO of a European postal service company. We are not talking about a specific company, but generally about a postal service provider operating in Europe. Generally speaking a US provider faces similar issues. Very specifically to Europe is the fact that previously existing national regulations have been lifted — any provider can now operate in almost every market or will be able to in the future. Direct competitors are usually parcel services like UPS or service providers entering from other countries.
prompt.question: The CEO is interested in the big picture of the market and does not care for detail analysis of a specific issue. What future trends would you expect for this business and industry, and how should the company position itself?

clarifying_info.q: What products and services does the company currently offer?
clarifying_info.a: The company offers traditional letters and packages (first-class letters, marketing mail, newspapers/magazines, packages), freight and forwarding (ocean, air, overland), supply chain management for retail/industry clients, and financial services such as retail banking and money transfers.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the main customers for the letter business?
clarifying_info.a: Private customers play only a minor role. The big customers are businesses such as banks, telecoms, and government agencies.

clarifying_info.q: Is the company currently operating on Sundays?
clarifying_info.a: No, the postal service client has previously not been operating on Sundays.

framework: Understand the current business: map all product/service lines and customer segments
Identify threats and risks to existing revenue streams (volume declines, digital substitution, cost pressures)
Identify opportunities in the traditional business model (new customers, new products, new geographies)
Value chain analysis: where in the chain does the company currently participate, and where could it integrate?

questions.prompt: What does the business of a typical European postal service provider look like? Describe the main product/service categories.
questions.guidance: A strong answer groups products into clear buckets: (1) Traditional Business — first-class letters, marketing mail, newspapers/magazines, packages; (2) Freight and Forwarding — ocean freight, air freight, industrial projects, overland freight (full and partial loads, trains and trucks); (3) Supply Chain Management — complete logistics for retail/industry clients including value-added services; (4) Financial Services — retail banking and money transfers. The interviewer should help the candidate group ideas into these defined categories.

questions.prompt: What problems or threats do you see with the existing traditional business? Which customer segment dominates volume?
questions.guidance: Key threats: (1) Letters — traditional letter volumes are declining year after year; private business is a minor share; large business customers (banks, telecoms, government) are moving to electronic communication; (2) Marketing mail — internet/email marketing increasingly replaces physical advertising brochures; (3) Newspapers and magazines — circulation is falling, publishers are going out of business; (4) Packages — no negative trends here, volume is stable or growing. Business customers dominate letter volumes.

questions.prompt: What opportunities do you see for the postal service provider?
questions.guidance: Opportunities include: (1) Traditional business — customers might outsource shipping to the postal service (e.g. newspapers outsourcing distribution); customers might also outsource printing; (2) Packages — increased internet shopping and business deliveries drive volume growth; offer pick-up stations and self-service options; consider grocery shipping; (3) General — cross-border M&A or organic growth to capture economies of scale (consolidation potential exists in the industry); cost savings via fleet overhaul and distribution reorganization.

questions.prompt: How does the value chain for marketing material look? Where does the postal service currently participate, and what integration opportunities exist?
questions.guidance: The value chain for marketing/promotional material runs: (1) Operating a business (e.g. retail) → (2) Deciding to promote a product/service → (3) Designing promotion materials → (4) Printing promotion materials → (5) Shipping promotion materials. Currently the client participates only in shipping. Backward integration into printing is very promising due to large economies of scale — some European postal service providers have already become the largest printers in their country. The postal service could also offer design services and demographic/targeting data to help clients identify target groups. A similar (though less integrated) value chain applies to newspapers/magazines and business letters.

questions.prompt: A publisher of magazines has approached the client to distribute his magazines on Sunday instead of Monday, hoping to grow his subscriber base. The postal service has not previously operated on Sundays. Do you think it would be a good idea to enhance operations to Sundays?
questions.guidance: The candidate should show business judgment by weighing incremental revenues against incremental costs. Most costs for the postal service are fixed on a given workday — what matters is whether a worker needs to go to a street at all, not how many items he delivers there. Key considerations: Additional revenues from distributing more magazines are minimal (e.g. roughly 10% more volume for that one publisher, but only a low number of additional subscribers is realistic). There is some possibility to increase prices for other products due to faster delivery, but this is marginal. Additional costs are significant: operating 7 days instead of 6 increases costs by up to ~16%. Conclusion: The cost increase (~16%) far outweighs the revenue upside (~10% for one customer), so Sunday delivery is not economically attractive.

math.setup: Current operating days = 6 days/week. Adding Sunday = 7 days/week. Cost increase = (7-6)/6 = 1/6 ≈ 16.7%. Revenue increase: one publisher gains ~10% more subscribers, but this is a small fraction of total revenue. Net impact is negative.
steps: Revenue increase ≈ 10% for one magazine publisher's volume (small fraction of total revenue)
Net impact: costs up ~16%, revenues up negligibly → not worthwhile
math.answer: Sunday operations are not economically justified; the ~16% cost increase far exceeds the minimal revenue gain.

brainstorming.prompt: What opportunities exist for the postal service to grow or defend its business?

categories.name: Traditional letter and mail business
ideas: Help large business customers manage physical-to-digital transition services
Offer hybrid mail (digital input, physical delivery)
Target remaining segments where physical mail is still required (legal, official)

categories.name: Marketing mail and printing
ideas: Backward integrate into printing marketing materials
Offer creative/design services for promotional campaigns
Provide demographic data and targeting analytics to help clients select target groups
Bundle printing + shipping into end-to-end campaign fulfillment

categories.name: Packages and e-commerce
ideas: Capitalize on internet shopping volume growth
Install self-service pick-up stations and parcel lockers
Offer returns management services for online retailers
Consider grocery and fresh food delivery

categories.name: New geographies and M&A
ideas: Cross-border M&A of other national postal service providers
Organic expansion into newly deregulated European markets
Leverage economies of scale across a larger geographic footprint

categories.name: Supply chain and logistics
ideas: Expand full supply chain management offering for retail and industrial clients
Add value-added services such as warehousing and last-mile fulfillment

categories.name: Financial services
ideas: Grow retail banking where branch networks are declining
Offer money transfer and payment services in underserved segments

recommendation: The CEO should pursue backward integration into the value chain, particularly in printing, to capture economies of scale and defend revenue as pure letter/mail volumes decline
The company should actively consider M&A of other European postal service providers to consolidate the market before competitors do so first
In parallel, invest in growing the packages and e-commerce logistics business, which faces no negative volume trends
risks: Other European postal service providers may act first on M&A, gaining a competitive advantage
Remaining national regulations and entrenched government-organization culture at acquisition targets could make integration difficult
Backward integration into printing requires capital investment and operational capabilities outside the core business
next_steps: Evaluate other European markets to identify M&A targets
Build a business case for a printing service offering, including economies of scale and pricing analysis
Assess the feasibility of self-service parcel infrastructure investments to capture e-commerce growth
